author: ribeye
dek: The national debt passed $40 trillion in mid-August, and one Zanesville man made the mistake of dividing it by every American alive.
disclaimer: Parody: the Barker family of Zanesville is fictional. The national debt passing $40 trillion is real, as reported by Reuters in 2026.
headline: Zanesville Man Does the Math on $40 Trillion, Immediately Regrets Doing the Math

ohio_quotes.quote: I divided forty trillion by everybody in America and got a number so big I had to sit down. I was already sitting down.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Dale Barker, Zanesville

ohio_quotes.quote: Our daughter found a house she loves and the mortgage rate is 7.4 percent. I told her when we bought ours it was 3. She looked at me like I'd told her we used to ride a dinosaur to school.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Ruth Barker, Zanesville

ohio_story: ZANESVILLE, Ohio — Dale Barker of Zanesville did everything right. He paid the electric bill on time, he kept the truck running, and he had never once, in 61 years, tried to divide a 14-digit number at the kitchen table. Then he read that the national debt had passed $40 trillion in mid-August, and, against his wife's explicit advice, he got out the calculator.

"Forty trillion divided by roughly 340 million Americans is about $118,000 apiece," Dale said, staring at the little screen like it had personally insulted him. "I did it twice, because the first time I thought I'd typed it wrong. I had not typed it wrong." Ruth, who had been enjoying a perfectly nice Tuesday, confiscated the calculator and suggested a walk along the Muskingum River instead, which Dale agreed to on the condition that nobody mention interest rates, the Y-Bridge, or the price of anything.

The real sting came later that evening, when their daughter called from Columbus about a little house she loves near the Muskingum County Fairgrounds. The mortgage rate on offer was 7.4 percent — the same kind of rate Reuters noted when the debt milestone landed — compared with the 3 percent rates common when the Barkers bought their own place in the 2010s. Dale has now started a spreadsheet titled "The Debt," which Ruth has renamed "Dale's Feelings" and hidden in a folder labeled "Do Not Open." The Barkers are coping the way Zanesville copes with everything: a porch, a glass of sweet tea, and a firm agreement not to do any more math until after football season.
real_summary: Total U.S. public debt outstanding reached approximately $40.047 trillion on August 18, 2026, the first time the national debt had ever crossed the $40 trillion mark, according to the U.S. Treasury's Debt to the Penny data. Of that total, about $32.266 trillion was held by the public and $7.782 trillion represented intragovernmental holdings, such as securities held by government trust funds.

Reuters reported in October that the debt had hit the $40 trillion milestone in August, as the Treasury reported a roughly $2 trillion budget deficit for the fiscal year ended September 30 — 12 percent larger than the previous year's and the biggest since the federal spending surge during the COVID-19 pandemic. The fiscal 2026 deficit was the third largest ever, with debt-service costs at a record $1.36 trillion, and government spending exceeded receipts by an amount equal to about 6.2 percent of the economy, against a roughly 3 percent level analysts consider sustainable.

Some of the $40 trillion total is owed to government entities like the Social Security Trust Fund, while the total owed to Treasury bondholders is around $32 trillion — rivaling the size of the economy. The debt-to-GDP ratio is now around 100 percent, a benchmark last seen during the financing of World War II. Rising borrowing costs are also reaching households: the rate on 30-year mortgages hit a recent high of 7.40 percent, according to Freddie Mac, compared with the ultra-low 3 percent rates common in the 2010s. Economists are largely split on whether the debt level itself is a problem, and say a U.S. debt default is highly unlikely.
source_note: Reuters reporting (Howard Schneider), Oct. 19, 2026: U.S. government debt hit $40 trillion in August 2026; fiscal 2026 deficit of about $2 trillion and record $1.36 trillion in debt-service costs. The precise Aug. 18 total of $40.047 trillion ($32.266 trillion held by the public, $7.782 trillion intragovernmental) is from the U.S. Treasury's Debt to the Penny data.
